title: A Major New Education Donor Avoids Some Pitfalls But Needs To Dig Deeper
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler examines MacKenzie Scott's no-strings gifts of billions to colleges serving disadvantaged students and finds the approach admirably trusting but aimed too late in the pipeline. She contrasts it with the earlier technology-fortune philanthropy that chased disruption and data, citing the Gates teacher-quality initiative that cost $575 million without improving teaching or learning. Her central claim is that education funders have attended to inputs like teacher quality and outputs like test scores while ignoring what actually happens inside classrooms, especially elementary ones. Because the seeds of inequity are planted in the early grades by the assumption that young children need not learn anything of substance, remedial gaps at college are the downstream symptom. She closes with three pieces of advice for donors: keep funding K-12, consult the cognitive science of learning, and respect data while recognizing its limits.
points: Gift-giving that skips grant proposals and reporting is a welcome change, but Wexler argues it leaves the root cause of college unpreparedness untouched.

Past reform philanthropy clustered around teacher quality, choice, accountability, standards and personalized learning, and the Gates teacher-evaluation effort failed despite its $575 million price tag.
Inequity begins in elementary classrooms where content-light instruction is the norm, so intervening at high school or college is already too late.
Educators' training has misled them about how learning works, so funders should look to psychologists and neuroscientists rather than relying solely on education insiders.
Data-driven education can mislead when schools measure illusory skills like making inferences and when studies are too short to detect knowledge-building effects.
quotes: Scott’s approach also steers clear of some of the high-handedness that has characterized major education funding in recent decades. A previous generation of philanthropists were often content to donate to education programs that looked good or tugged at their heartstrings.

These funders have tended to cluster around the same few ideas for K-12 schools: improving teacher quality, expanding school choice, holding schools and teachers accountable on the basis of reading and math scores, beefing up academic standards, and shifting to “personalized learning.

The total cost was $575 million, with a third borne by Gates. But the effort failed to boost teacher quality or student learning, and one commentator argued that it was correlated with a significant negative effect on test scores.

A huge challenge for colleges like those Scott is funding is that so many students arrive unprepared for college-level work. On average, 60% of students who enroll in community college take one or more remedial courses within three years; among those who are low-income, the figure is 76%. Most who start remedial courses never complete them—and never get a degree.

But the seeds of inequity are being planted in elementary classrooms on a daily basis, largely because of the deeply mistaken assumption that it’s not important for younger kids to learn anything of substance. The result is that the gaps between demographic groups that are present in kindergarten only get wider and harder to narrow as grade levels go up.

Researchers in other fields who study learning—primarily psychologists and neurologists—have made great advances in recent decades that have not penetrated the world of education. To be sure, findings from scientific studies can’t tell teachers exactly what to do in classrooms. But they can guide us in figuring out what’s likely to work and what’s not.

Data-driven” education may sound good, but much of the data collected in schools focuses on largely illusory skills like “making inferences” and not on whether students have learned anything substantive; faulty data may lead only to continued faulty instruction.
